opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in terms of generality across the full range of human cognitive capabilities. The human brain is the only existence proof we have of a general intelligence, so for me the bar is a system that can do essentially all the cognitive things humans can do, and do them consistently, not just in a few showcase areas.

Today's systems are impressive. They can solve hard math problems or write code, but then they'll fail at something quite simple if you pose it a slightly different way. That jaggedness, being superhuman in some areas and surprisingly brittle in others, tells you we're not there yet. A true AGI shouldn't have those obvious holes.

In practice, I'd want a very broad battery of tests, thousands of them, covering reasoning, planning, memory, creativity, physical intuition, and so on. On top of that, I'd want what I'd call a lighthouse moment: something like inventing a new scientific conjecture, or coming up with a game as deep and elegant as Go, rather than just playing it brilliantly. That kind of genuine invention, not just problem-solving, would be a strong signal.

I'd also give it some time. You'd want top experts to spend months probing it and trying to find weaknesses. If they can't easily find any, and it really does seem to match human capability across the board, then I think you could reasonably call it AGI.

r001.rationale: The response sets the bar at doing essentially all the cognitive things humans can do and identifies the human brain as the example of general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says the system should perform consistently across capabilities and should not have obvious holes or jaggedness across domains.

r003.rationale: It proposes thousands of tests spanning reasoning, planning, memory, creativity, and other cognitive abilities.

r004.rationale: It says top experts should spend months probing for weaknesses, and that their inability to find them would support calling the system AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to go back to the original definition that we had when we started DeepMind, which was a system that's capable of exhibiting all the cognitive capabilities that humans have. And the reason that's the right reference point, I think, is that the human mind is the only existence proof we have that general intelligence is possible. So it's not an arbitrary benchmark, it's actually the only one that's grounded in something real.

Now, what does that mean in practice? I think you'd want a system that can do, let's say, the full range of things a human can do with their mind. Not just the things that are easy to test or easy to verify. And I would put a lot of emphasis on consistency. One of the things we see with today's systems, and this is true of our own systems too, is that they can do incredibly impressive things, win a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad, say, and then make quite trivial mistakes on a high school maths problem or a simple logic puzzle that a child could do. So there's a kind of jaggedness to the capability profile. A truly general system shouldn't have those holes. It should be robust across the board in a way that a well-educated human is.

The second thing I'd look for is the ability to learn new things efficiently and continually. Humans can pick up a new skill from a handful of examples, or a new domain from a few books, and integrate that into everything else they know. Current systems are still quite data-hungry and quite brittle when it comes to online learning. So I'd want to see that kind of sample efficiency.

And then the thing I actually care most about, personally, is invention. Can the system come up with a genuinely new conjecture, not just solve a hard problem that someone else posed? Could it have invented general relativity given what Einstein knew in 1915? Could it have come up with the game of Go, rather than just playing it superbly? That's a much higher bar than most of the current benchmarks, and I think it's the real test. Because once you have a system that can do that, you've got something that can really contribute to the scientific process rather than just accelerate it.

In terms of how you'd actually measure it, I don't think there's going to be a single test. It's more like you'd want a battery of thousands of tasks across all cognitive domains, and you'd probably want a few hundred of the world's best experts spending a sustained period, months, trying to find holes in it. If they can't find any, if there's no obvious weakness that a human can readily exploit, then I'd say you're probably there. My own view is that we're a few years away from that still, maybe five to ten, and I think some of the components, the continual learning, the long-term planning, the real creativity, those are still missing and may need one or two more breakthroughs rather than just scale.

r001.rationale: Defines AGI as exhibiting all the cognitive capabilities humans have and doing the full range of things a human can do with their mind.

r002.rationale: Explicitly emphasizes consistency across capabilities and says a truly general system should not have holes in its capability profile.

r003.rationale: Proposes a battery of thousands of tasks across all cognitive domains.

r004.rationale: Says that if a few hundred top experts examine the system for months and cannot find holes or an obvious exploitable weakness, it is probably there.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is generality. We have systems that are extraordinarily good at particular things, but the question is whether a single system can learn and operate across the broad range of cognitive tasks that humans can do, including situations it’s never encountered before.

So I wouldn’t rely on one benchmark, or even on something like the Turing test. I’d want to see a whole range of evaluations, particularly involving genuinely new problems. Can it transfer knowledge from one domain to another? Can it plan, reason, and revise its understanding when the evidence changes? And can it do those things reliably, rather than just occasionally producing a brilliant answer?

Scientific discovery would be a particularly compelling demonstration for me: a system that could formulate an original hypothesis, work out how to test it, and arrive at a discovery. That would help distinguish understanding and invention from reproducing things it has already seen. But ultimately, it’s the breadth and flexibility of the capability that would make it general.

r001.rationale: The response describes AGI as learning and operating across the broad range of cognitive tasks humans can do, which communicates the full-range capability target.

r002.rationale: It says the system should transfer knowledge across domains and perform reliably rather than only occasionally, communicating consistent capability across domains.

r003.rationale: It proposes a whole range of evaluations, especially on new problems, and frames the target as the broad range of cognitive tasks humans can do.

r004.rationale: It does not mention leading subject experts examining the system over time or their inability to find an obvious flaw.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is generality. Can the system learn and perform across the full range of cognitive tasks that humans can, including tasks it hasn’t encountered before? And can it transfer what it learns in one domain to another, rather than needing us to build a separate solution each time?

I wouldn’t judge that from a single benchmark or an impressive conversation. I’d want a broad set of tests, particularly novel problems where memorization isn’t enough. Scientific discovery would be a compelling test: can it formulate a useful hypothesis, work out how to test it, and revise its understanding when the evidence contradicts it?

So the standard would be robust, flexible competence across domains. We’d need to see that consistently, rather than infer it from a few remarkable demonstrations.

r001.rationale: Defines AGI by learning and performing across the full range of cognitive tasks humans can, including unfamiliar tasks.

r002.rationale: Requires robust, flexible competence across domains and says it should be demonstrated consistently.

r003.rationale: Suggests a broad set of tests, but does not clearly propose a large-scale battery of cognitive tasks humans can perform.

r004.rationale: Does not mention leading experts examining the system or their inability to find flaws as evidence of generality.
